<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

  /* Reading mode hides the chrome and the empty .arxiv-html-header marker: the pinned JS reads
     the marker's display to know which way to toggle. The marker draws no box. */
  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }
  html[data-reading-mode="enabled"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }
  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme
     icon by making its span a block). */
  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }
  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;
     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white
     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as
     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */
  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }
  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }

  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows
     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the
     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and
     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).
     The controls show their names. */
  @media (min-width: 1280px) {
    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }
  }
  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen
     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky
     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box
     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in
     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side
     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */
  @media (max-width: 1279px) {
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }
    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }
    html:not([data-toc-display="block"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }
    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }
    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }
  }

</ol></li>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jaeseok Byun<sup id="id1" class="ltx_sup">1,2 🖂</sup>
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Gukyeong Kwon<sup id="id2" class="ltx_sup">2 🖂</sup>
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Han-Kai Hsu<sup id="id3" class="ltx_sup">2</sup>
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Meher Gitika Karumuri<sup id="id4" class="ltx_sup">2</sup>
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Zhikang Zhang<sup id="id5" class="ltx_sup">2</sup>
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Hao Yang<sup id="id6" class="ltx_sup">2</sup>
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Davide Modolo<sup id="id7" class="ltx_sup">2 🖂</sup>
</span></span>
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author"><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Seoul National University, South Korea
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Amazon AGI, USA
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>
</span>
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_email"><span class="ltx_contact_name">E-mail </span><a href="mailto:wotjr3868@snu.ac.kr,%20gukyeong@amazon.com,%20dmodolo@amazon.com">wotjr3868@snu.ac.kr, gukyeong@amazon.com, dmodolo@amazon.com</a>
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Upgrading embedding models typically requires expensive database re-indexing, as new query embeddings are incompatible with existing database embeddings. While Backward Compatible Training (BCT) mitigates this by enforcing compatibility during training, existing approaches often require updating the backbone model. This is impractical because of significant training cost, the risk of performance regression, and limited access to proprietary model weights. We introduce Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter  (<span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MKP-Adapter</span>), the first adapter-only BCT approach for Multi-Modal Large Language Models (MLLMs) that requires no backbone updates. We identified that the primary challenge in adapter-only BCT is preserving the knowledge of the new embeddings while enforcing backward compatibility. Hence, we propose a multi-level preservation loss that maintains the geometric structure of the embedding spaces throughout BCT. Furthermore, a focal re-weighting strategy is integrated to prioritize learning from challenging samples. Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves strong backward compatibility across diverse multi-modal benchmarks (image, text, visual document, and video retrieval tasks) and model types. Notably, MKP-Adapter is trained solely on pre-extracted embeddings and requires only negligible additional latency relative to the original backbone forward pass, highlighting its efficiency.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Embedding compatibility Multi-modal retrieval Adapter
</div><span id="footnotex1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span>This work was conducted during Jaeseok Byun’s internship at Amazon.</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Embedding models have become fundamental components in modern information retrieval systems, enabling semantic search across diverse data modalities, including text, images, audio, and video <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>. However, when a new model is trained independently of an old model for performance improvement, the embeddings produced by the two models are not inherently compatible. This incompatibility forces systems to rebuild their entire embedding database, a process known as “backfilling”, which typically requires heavy computational overhead, especially for large-scale retrieval systems.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To address this challenge, the Backward Compatible Training (BCT) paradigm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite> has been introduced. To be specific, these approaches incorporate explicit backward compatibility constraints into the training objective of the new models and allow the new embeddings to be used for querying databases constructed with old embedding models. Because compatibility constraints must be incorporated during the training stage of the new embedding model, existing BCT methods cannot be applied to pre-trained models and thus require retraining from scratch to achieve compatibility. A recent approach, XBT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>, attempts to avoid such full retraining through a two-phase procedure: it first trains an adapter on text-only data to bridge old and new embeddings and then applies LoRA-tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite> to the new model backbone using contrastive learning. Although XBT reports promising compatibility results on CLIP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> under standard cross-modal retrieval settings, XBT still requires backbone updates.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">BCT approaches that require backbone updates, via LoRA-tuning or full retraining, suffer from several crucial limitations, particularly in the context of MLLMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>, <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>.
First, high computational cost. Backbone updates require repeated forward and backward passes and become prohibitively expensive for large-scale modern foundation models.
Second, the risk of degrading model capability.
LoRA-tuning the new model may disturb pre-trained knowledge, while training the new model from scratch with compatibility constraints can compromise the original training objectives as observed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>.
Mitigating these risks requires carefully designed BCT strategies and high-quality large-scale training data. Third, limited applicability due to weight access requirements. Backbone updates require direct access to model weights, making such approaches inapplicable to proprietary API based models that only support black box inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To that end, we propose a practical alternative that achieves backward compatibility by training only an adapter (shown in <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(a)), without requiring any backbone updates. This adapter-only approach resolves aforementioned issues as follows.
First, it operates solely on pre-extracted embeddings and requires no forward or backward passes through the backbone, making it efficient for training and readily applicable to MLLMs.
Second, the pre-trained backbone remains intact, which allows to avoid performance regression and knowledge disturbance.
Third, it requires no access to model weights, enabling direct deployment with API based models.
While this adapter-only approach offers clear practical advantages over prior BCT methods, learning an adapter that achieves strong backward compatibility remains challenging.
Unlike previous BCT approaches that jointly update or LoRA-tune the backbone to enforce compatibility while maintaining discriminative capability, our adapter-only setting requires the adapter alone to satisfy both objectives, with the backbone kept frozen.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2609.16875v1/figures/overview_ours.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/111;" width="476" height="111" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> <span id="S1.F1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Overview of MKP-Adapter</span>. </span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">A naive approach to obtaining such an adapter is to train it by directly projecting new embeddings onto old ones (<em id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g</em>.<span id="S1.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text"></span>, via <math id="S1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L1</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L2</annotation></semantics></math> loss). However, forcing projected embeddings to match weaker or noisier old targets can lose the improved representational structure of the new model, which in turn can undermine backward compatibility performance.
Our key idea is therefore to preserve the knowledge encoded in the new embeddings after projection.
As illustrated in <a href="#S1.F1" title="In 1 Introduction ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(b), we achieve this by combining the base projection loss (shown in red) with multi-level preservation regularization (shown in purple) at three granularities:
(1) <em id="S1.p5.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">point-wise</em>, a cycle-consistency loss that reconstructs each original embedding from its projected embedding;
(2) <em id="S1.p5.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">distance-wise</em>, a loss that preserves relative distances between embedding pairs; and
(3) <em id="S1.p5.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">angle-wise</em>, a loss that preserves angular relations among embedding triplets.
Finally, to account for varying preservation difficulty across modalities and semantic contexts, we apply a focal re-weighting scheme that emphasizes harder samples.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct a comprehensive evaluation under two practical model upgrade scenarios:
(1) upgrading from dual-tower models (<em id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g</em>.<span id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text"></span>, CLIP<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>) to MLLMs (<em id="S1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g</em>.<span id="S1.p6.1.4" class="ltx_text"></span>, GME<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite>), and (2) upgrading between different versions of MLLMs.
Our method achieves effective backward compatibility across diverse model upgrade scenarios on standard image-text retrieval benchmarks, including MS-COCO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>, Flickr30K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>, and Urban1K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>.
We further show that our approach generalizes across diverse tasks and modalities, including instruction-following queries in MMEB <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>, visual document retrieval on ViDoRe <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, and video retrieval on MSR-VTT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite>, VATEX <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite>, and MSVD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>.
Across all benchmarks, our method consistently and considerably outperforms baseline approaches in terms of backward compatibility.
Moreover, the adapter adds only negligible overhead to the total system inference pipeline (0.01% of the original backbone forward pass cost) and can be trained within 1–2 hours on a moderate-scale (558k paired) dataset (see <a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Analyses ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a>) on 8 A100 GPUs, demonstrating the practicality and efficiency of our approach.
Overall, our contributions are summarized as follows:</p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce the first adapter-only BCT framework across multiple modalities (image, text, visual documents, and video), particularly suited for using MLLMs as query encoders.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a multi-level knowledge preservation loss to maintain the representation quality of the embeddings when training for backward compatibility. Our comprehensive evaluation validates the effectiveness of the proposed loss on diverse modalities and model upgrade scenarios.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MKP-Adapter can be trained within a few hours using pre-extracted embeddings and incurs only negligible overhead to the overall inference pipeline.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Multi-modal embedding models</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Early multi-modal embedding models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>, <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>]</cite> adopt dual-tower architectures trained on large-scale noisy web image-text data. Following LLaVA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>, which connects a large language model to a frozen visual backbone, various MLLM variants <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>]</cite> have shown strong performance on multi-modal generation tasks. Several works have since extended MLLMs to embedding-based retrieval: E5-V <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> fine-tunes MLLMs with contrastive learning on text-only data, while GME <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite> leverages large-scale image, text, and image-text composition data. VLM2Vec <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> is trained on a carefully curated dataset called the Massive Multimodal Embedding Benchmark (MMEB) training set and achieves strong performance on the corresponding MMEB evaluation benchmark.
UniME <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> further improves by using knowledge distillation and hard negative mining.
In this work, we consider compatibility scenarios spanning these diverse MLLM-based query encoders.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Embedding compatibility</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Two representative paradigms have been proposed for embedding compatibility: forward compatible training (FCT) and backward compatible training (BCT).
The pioneering FCT work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite> converts old database embeddings to be compatible with a new model via lightweight adapters, but relies on auxiliary features from a separate model, which are often unavailable in practice.
FastFill <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite> considers online backfilling by estimating the appropriate ordering of the backfilling sample. RBT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite> updates both query and database embeddings using a unified adapter. Recently, Embedding Converter <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> achieves strong forward compatibility for text embeddings by leveraging relative distance information.
While FCT only requires training a lightweight adapter, it necessitates converting all database embeddings through the adapter, which can incur substantial computational overhead at massive scale database. Lightweight adapters have also been explored for task and domain adaptation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>, <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>, but these methods focus on transforming embeddings within a single model rather than maintaining compatibility across model upgrades.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast, BCT modifies the training procedure of the new model to ensure compatibility with a fixed gallery of old embeddings, avoiding database updates.
However, incorporating backward compatibility constraints can degrade the discriminative capability of the new model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>.
Prior works mitigate this by aligning class centers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>, expanding embedding dimensionality <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite>, or introducing alignment losses <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>.
These methods require compatibility to be enforced during training, making them unsuitable for frozen pre-trained models and largely limited to unimodal settings.
XBT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite> extends BCT to cross-modal settings via LoRA tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite>, enabling application to frozen models, but it still requires updating the backbone parameters.
In contrast, we propose an adapter-only backward compatibility approach that requires neither backbone modification nor weight access, making it well-suited for using MLLMs as query encoders across diverse retrieval scenarios. We note our method is not tied to any specific model architecture or modality, as it operates directly on pre-extracted embeddings.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Problem Settings</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Problem formulation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our goal is to learn a mapping function from the new embedding space to the old embedding space for backward compatibility, defined as <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h:\mathbb{R}^{d^{new}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d^{old}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msup></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h:\mathbb{R}^{d^{new}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d^{old}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Let <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{old}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>old</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{old}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="f_{\text{new}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>new</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f_{\text{new}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the frozen pre-trained old and new embedding models, respectively. The corresponding embeddings are given by <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{old}}=f{{}_{\text{old}}}(s_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mtext>old</mtext></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mmultiscripts><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mprescripts></mprescripts><mtext>old</mtext><mrow></mrow></mmultiscripts></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{old}}=f{{}_{\text{old}}}(s_{i})</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{new}}=f_{\text{new}}(s_{i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mtext>new</mtext></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mtext>new</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{new}}=f_{\text{new}}(s_{i})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes a data sample.
The dataset spans multiple modalities (images, text, visual documents, and videos).
To reflect realistic deployment settings, we assume all embeddings are pre-extracted, requiring no additional forward passes through either embedding model during training.
All embeddings are <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L2</annotation></semantics></math>-normalized before any adapter operations or indexing.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Base adapter</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A naive approach to training such an adapter is to learn a mapping <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h:\mathbb{R}^{d^{new}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d^{old}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msup></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h:\mathbb{R}^{d^{new}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d^{old}}</annotation></semantics></math> by minimizing the L2 loss (mean squared error) between the projected embedding and the old embedding, such that <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new})\approx\mathbf{x}_{i}^{old}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new})\approx\mathbf{x}_{i}^{old}</annotation></semantics></math>. Here, <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d^{new}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d^{new}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d^{old}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d^{old}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the dimensionalities of the new and old embedding models, respectively.
Formally, given <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> samples, we minimize the distance between embeddings:</p>
<table id="S3.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{base}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new})-\mathbf{x}_{i}^{old}\|_{2}^{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{base}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new})-\mathbf{x}_{i}^{old}\|_{2}^{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While we use mean squared error in this formulation, alternative distance metrics such as mean absolute error may also be employed.
We note that while FCT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite> applies such a mapping in the opposite direction (old <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> new), our backward compatibility setting reverses this direction by projecting new embeddings into the old space (new <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> old).
For multi-modal retrieval scenarios such as image–text retrieval, we form the training set by aggregating pre-extracted embeddings from different modalities into a unified dataset. Consequently, each mini-batch contains embeddings from multiple modalities, and the adapter <math id="S3.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> is trained in a modality-agnostic manner using a single shared mapping across modalities. More details and alternative adapter design choices are provided in the supplementary materials (S.M).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Method</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Motivation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike knowledge distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite> or forward-compatible training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>]</cite>, which use newer or stronger embeddings as the supervision target, an adapter-only BCT is inherently more challenging. Specifically, the base loss <math id="S4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{base}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>base</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{base}}</annotation></semantics></math> in <a href="#S3.E1" title="In 3.2 Base adapter ‣ 3 Problem Settings ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> encourages new embeddings to fit the old embedding space as the target, which typically exhibits a weaker and noisier semantic structure than the new one.
Therefore, using old embeddings as the target naively forces the new embeddings to follow this noisy structure, which can sacrifice the discriminative capacity of the new model and potentially lead to poor backward compatibility performance.
Our key insight is that, rather than simply fitting into the old space, the projection should preserve the semantic structure and knowledge encoded in the new embeddings. Building upon the base loss, we add regularization losses that explicitly preserve the representation quality of the embeddings before and after the projection. In particular, we introduce multi-level preservation losses that maintain the refined similarity structure of the new embeddings at increasing geometric complexity, along with a focal re-weighting strategy that prioritizes challenging samples for improving robustness and generalization.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Multi-level preservation loss</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Point-wise preservation loss]</span>
We first introduce a point-wise preservation loss inspired by cycle consistency <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite> to ensure that individual embedding information is preserved after projection. The core idea is that if the projected embedding can be reconstructed back to the original, the essential information of the original embedding is preserved.
To achieve this, we introduce an auxiliary adapter <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g:\mathbb{R}^{d^{old}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d^{new}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msup></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g:\mathbb{R}^{d^{old}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d^{new}}</annotation></semantics></math> that maps embeddings from the old space back to the new space.
For each embedding, we project the new embedding to the old space via the main adapter <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h:\mathbb{R}^{d^{new}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d^{old}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msup></msup><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><msup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h:\mathbb{R}^{d^{new}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d^{old}}</annotation></semantics></math>, then reconstruct it back to the new space via <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math>. By minimizing the reconstruction error, we enforce that <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> maintains sufficient semantic information needed to recover the original embedding. Formally, we train two adapters jointly with the following point-level loss:</p>
<table id="S4.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{point}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|g(h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new}))-\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new}\|_{2}^{2}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{point}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\|g(h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new}))-\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new}\|_{2}^{2}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><math id="S4.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> is used only for training and <math id="S4.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math> is the learned adapter used during inference.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Distance-wise preservation loss]</span>
While the point-wise loss preserves information at the level of individual embeddings, it does not explicitly enforce the preservation of relationships between embeddings, which are crucial for retrieval tasks where relative similarities determine ranking.
Inspired by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, we introduce an additional distance-wise preservation loss that maintains relative distances between embeddings, thereby encouraging the model to preserve the relative similarity structure of the original embeddings in the projected space.
To capture comprehensive pairwise mutual relationships, we follow <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> and consider both global distances computed over randomly sampled pairs within each batch, and local distances computed based on the precomputed <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>-nearest neighbors of each sample selected in the <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">new</span> embedding space (<math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=100</annotation></semantics></math>). Further details are provided in S.M.
While this formulation resembles techniques used in knowledge distillation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, a key distinction is that, instead of learning from an external teacher model that typically provides a stronger supervisory signal, we use the original new embeddings themselves as self-targets to preserve their inherent relational structure during projection.
We define the distance-wise structure preservation loss as:</p>
<table id="S4.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{distance}=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}}\left|Dist(h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new}),h(\mathbf{x}_{j}^{new}))-Dist(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new},\mathbf{x}_{j}^{new})\right|," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><mo>|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{distance}=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}}\left|Dist(h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new}),h(\mathbf{x}_{j}^{new}))-Dist(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new},\mathbf{x}_{j}^{new})\right|,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes anchor–reference pairs <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(i,j)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(i,j)</annotation></semantics></math>, with <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> sampled from the mini-batch and <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> chosen either randomly within the batch (global) or from the <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> nearest neighbors of <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> (local). The distance function is defined as <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Dist(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})=1-\cos(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐛</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝐚</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐛</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Dist(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})=1-\cos(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\cos(\cdot,\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos(\cdot,\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes cosine similarity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Angle-wise preservation loss]</span>
To further preserve the relative similarity structure, we incorporate an angle-wise loss inspired by relational knowledge distillation (RKD) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>.
While distance-based losses are defined by pairs of embeddings, angle-wise losses incorporate triplets.
By leveraging the higher-order structural information provided by these additional embeddings, we hypothesize that angle-wise regularization complements distance preservation in maintaining the overall manifold structure.
As with the previous losses (<a href="#S4.E2" title="In 4.2 Multi-level preservation loss ‣ 4 Method ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eqs.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and <a href="#S4.E3" title="Equation 3 ‣ 4.2 Multi-level preservation loss ‣ 4 Method ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), our formulation is self-supervised; unlike RKD, which uses a strong teacher as the target, we preserve the angles defined by the new embeddings themselves after projection.
Given a triplet of embeddings, the angle formed at the vertex <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as:</p>
<table id="S4.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\psi_{A}(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{j},\mathbf{x}_{k})=\cos\angle\mathbf{x}_{i}\mathbf{x}_{j}\mathbf{x}_{k}=\langle\mathbf{e}^{ij},\mathbf{e}^{kj}\rangle," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>ψ</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∠</mi></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐞</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐞</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\psi_{A}(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{j},\mathbf{x}_{k})=\cos\angle\mathbf{x}_{i}\mathbf{x}_{j}\mathbf{x}_{k}=\langle\mathbf{e}^{ij},\mathbf{e}^{kj}\rangle,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{e}^{ij}=\frac{\mathbf{x}_{i}-\mathbf{x}_{j}}{\|\mathbf{x}_{i}-\mathbf{x}_{j}\|_{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐞</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{e}^{ij}=\frac{\mathbf{x}_{i}-\mathbf{x}_{j}}{\|\mathbf{x}_{i}-\mathbf{x}_{j}\|_{2}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{e}^{kj}=\frac{\mathbf{x}_{k}-\mathbf{x}_{j}}{\|\mathbf{x}_{k}-\mathbf{x}_{j}\|_{2}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐞</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{e}^{kj}=\frac{\mathbf{x}_{k}-\mathbf{x}_{j}}{\|\mathbf{x}_{k}-\mathbf{x}_{j}\|_{2}}</annotation></semantics></math> are normalized directional vectors. This measures the angle at <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> formed by the triplet <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{j},\mathbf{x}_{k})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{j},\mathbf{x}_{k})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The angle-wise preservation loss then maintains these angular relationships after projection:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
