<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒯</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{T}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the set of embedding triplets formed using global (random) and local (nearest-neighbor) sampling.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Together, the multi-level preservation loss function is defined as:</p>
<table id="S4.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{multi-preservation}=\mathcal{L}_{point}+\mathcal{L}_{distance}+\mathcal{L}_{angle}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{multi-preservation}=\mathcal{L}_{point}+\mathcal{L}_{distance}+\mathcal{L}_{angle}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Focal re-weighting strategy</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For more effective training, we employ a focal re-weighting strategy into the multi-level preservation losses (<a href="#S4.E6" title="In 4.2 Multi-level preservation loss ‣ 4 Method ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>). Preservation difficulty might vary across modalities and semantics, with some samples being easily aligned while others remain challenging. Without re-weighting, easy samples can dominate the training loss, preventing the adapter from adequately learning difficult cases.
Inspired by focal loss in object detection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, we re-weight the loss term based on errors between original and reconstructed embeddings to emphasize challenging examples. For example, the focal-weighted point-level loss is defined as:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S4.E7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{point}^{focal}&amp;=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}\Delta_{i},\\
\text{where}\quad&amp;\Delta_{i}=||g(h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new}))-\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new}||_{2}^{2},\quad w_{i}=\left(\frac{\Delta_{i}}{\bar{\Delta}}\right)^{\gamma},\quad\bar{\Delta}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Delta_{i}.\end{split}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable columnspacing="0pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msubsup></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_right" columnalign="right"><mtext>where</mtext></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><mo fence="false">|</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow><mi>γ</mi></msup></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>N</mi></munderover><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{point}^{focal}&amp;=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{i}\Delta_{i},\\
\text{where}\quad&amp;\Delta_{i}=||g(h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new}))-\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new}||_{2}^{2},\quad w_{i}=\left(\frac{\Delta_{i}}{\bar{\Delta}}\right)^{\gamma},\quad\bar{\Delta}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Delta_{i}.\end{split}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> is the focusing parameter that controls the strength of re-weighting, with <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma=0</annotation></semantics></math> corresponding to no re-weighting and larger values placing more emphasis on harder samples.
We apply the same focal re-weighting strategy to the distance-wise and angle-wise preservation losses defined in <a href="#S4.E3" title="In 4.2 Multi-level preservation loss ‣ 4 Method ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eqs.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and <a href="#S4.E5" title="Equation 5 ‣ 4.2 Multi-level preservation loss ‣ 4 Method ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>; formal definitions are provided in S.M.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we obtain our model, dubbed MKP-Adapter, by optimizing the following training objective, which combines all proposed loss components:</p>
<table id="S4.E8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{total}=\mathcal{L}_{base}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{multi-preservation}^{focal}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{total}=\mathcal{L}_{base}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{multi-preservation}^{focal},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.p3.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{multi-preservation}}^{focal}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>multi-preservation</mtext><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{multi-preservation}}^{focal}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the combined multi-level preservation losses with focal re-weighting, and <math id="S4.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> controls the trade-off between projection onto the old embedding space and preservation of the new embedding capabilities.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Experimental Results</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the compatibility performance of MKP-Adapter across diverse upgrade scenarios and modalities. We first demonstrate its effectiveness on standard image-to-text (I2T) and text-to-image (T2I) cross-modal retrieval tasks. Beyond retrieval, we also assess performance on complex MMEB benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>, which includes a range of embedding-dependent tasks such as classification, visual grounding, and visual question answering. We further extend our evaluation to additional modalities such as visual document and video.
We consider two representative model upgrade scenarios from old to new embedding models:
(1) Dual-tower <math id="S5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> MLLM, upgrading from traditional dual-tower architectures to MLLMs, where CLIP ViT-L/14 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> is used as the old model, and UniME (7B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> (or GME (7B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite>) as the new model; and
(2) MLLM <math id="S5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> MLLM, upgrading between MLLM variants, where E5-V (7B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> is used as the old model, and UniME (7B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> as the new model.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Experimental settings</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Training setup]</span>
To obtain training embeddings for image and text retrieval, we use the LLaVA-LCS image–text paired dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>, which contains approximately 558K image–text pairs. From this dataset, we construct three types of training inputs: (1) images only, (2) texts only, and (3) image+text compositions where paired image–text samples are provided jointly as input to the MLLM. The composition inputs are included to better support instruction-following scenarios in the MMEB benchmark, where queries combine both textual and visual information.
As described in <a href="#S4" title="4 Method ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, we aggregate all inputs into a unified training set for adapter training. During training, inputs are randomly sampled to form mini-batches across diverse modalities. Additional details and ablations, including results without composition data, are provided in S.M.
We further experiment with larger datasets, SBU <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite> (1M pairs) and CC3M <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite> (3M pairs), to analyze the effect of training data scale on compatibility performance.
For visual document retrieval, we use the ColPali training set <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, which contains approximately 118K paired samples. Each visual document is treated as a single image during both training and evaluation.
For video retrieval, we use a subset of the LLaVA-Hound video dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite> with approximately 300K paired samples. To obtain video embeddings, we uniformly sample 8 frames from each video, extract embeddings for each frame independently, and then average them to form a single video representation, following prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We use a 2-layer MLP as our adapter architecture with the following structure: LayerNorm-Linear-GELU-Dropout(0.1)-Linear.
The default hidden dimension is set to be equal to the input embedding dimension.
We train the adapter using the AdamW optimizer <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite> with a weight decay of <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-4}</annotation></semantics></math>, a batch size of 32, and an initial learning rate of <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10^{-3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>10</mn><mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10^{-3}</annotation></semantics></math>.
A cosine annealing learning rate schedule is applied, decaying the learning rate from the initial value to zero, without warmup.
All experiments are conducted on 8 A100 (40GB) GPUs.
We use the <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L2</annotation></semantics></math> loss as the default base projection loss defined in <a href="#S3.E1" title="In 3.2 Base adapter ‣ 3 Problem Settings ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, although our preservation regularization can be combined with alternative base losses.
Both <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S5.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> are set to 1.0 by default.
Additional training details are provided in S.M.
Results under diverse hyperparameter choices are reported in <a href="#Pt0.A2.T3" title="In B.3 Batch size ablation ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tabs.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S3</span></a> and <a href="#Pt0.A2.T10" title="Table S10 ‣ B.8 Hyper-parameters ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S10</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Evaluation setup]</span>
We evaluate the backward compatibility performance of MKP-Adapter across multiple benchmarks, where query embeddings are computed as <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h(\mathbf{x}^{new})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h(\mathbf{x}^{new})</annotation></semantics></math> using the adapter trained by each method, while database embeddings remain fixed as <math id="S5.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}^{old}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}^{old}</annotation></semantics></math> from the old model. We follow the official evaluation protocols and metrics of each benchmark for comparability with prior works. First, we demonstrate its effectiveness on standard I2T and T2I retrieval using MS-COCO <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>]</cite>, Flickr30K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>, and Urban1K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>, reporting Recall@1. Additional Recall@10 results are provided in <a href="#Pt0.A5.T14" title="In E.2 Additional R@10 results corresponding to ‣ Appendix E Additional evaluation ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S14</span></a>, and large-scale evaluation results on the full COCO validation set are reported in <a href="#Pt0.A5.T15" title="In E.3 Large retrieval evaluation (COCO val entire set) ‣ Appendix E Additional evaluation ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S15</span></a>.
Second, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation on MMEB, a more challenging benchmark comprising 36 datasets across four task categories (classification, VQA, retrieval, and visual grounding).
We note this evaluation assesses the generalization ability of the adapters across diverse tasks and domains, as MMEB includes sub-datasets drawn from domains substantially different from the training data.
Moreover, the queries contain explicit instructions, allowing us to evaluate instruction-following capability as well.
Following standard protocols, we report Precision@1 as the metric.
Third, we evaluate text-to-visual-document retrieval on ViDoRe (V1) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, a benchmark of 10 sub-datasets spanning various content types (text, figures, infographics, tables) and domains (medical, business, scientific, administrative). Following prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, we report nDCG@5 as the evaluation metric.
Finally, we assess video retrieval performance on three benchmarks: MSR-VTT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite>, MSVD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>]</cite>, and VATEX <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite>, using Recall@1 as the metric. We report results only for CLIP<math id="S5.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>GME on document and video retrieval benchmarks, as UniME is not suitable as the new model due to its weak performance on both benchmarks (see <a href="#Pt0.A2.SS9" title="B.9 Exclusion of UniME in . ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B.9</span></a>).</p>
</div>

</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Baselines]</span> To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has explored adapter-only approaches for backward compatibility in multimodal retrieval. We therefore establish three adapter-only baselines for comparison, adapted from related literature, in which only the adapter is trained while both the old and new embedding models remain frozen.</p>
<ul id="S5.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S5.I1.ix1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(a)</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.ix1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.ix1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Base adapter <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>. This adapter is trained using the <math id="S5.I1.ix1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L2</annotation></semantics></math> loss defined in <a href="#S3.E1" title="In 3.2 Base adapter ‣ 3 Problem Settings ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
We adopt <math id="S5.I1.ix1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L2</annotation></semantics></math> instead of <math id="S5.I1.ix1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L1</annotation></semantics></math>, as it consistently yields superior performance in our experiments (See <a href="#Pt0.A2.T5" title="In B.5 Different base adapters ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S5</span></a>).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.ix2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(b)</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.ix2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.ix2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">EC-style adapter <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>.
Embedding Converter (EC) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite> achieves state-of-the-art performance in forward-compatible training (FCT) for text retrieval (old <math id="S5.I1.ix2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> new) by distilling relative distance information between embeddings in addition to the <math id="S5.I1.ix2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L2</annotation></semantics></math> loss.
We adopt this method to the reverse direction (new <math id="S5.I1.ix2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> old) to establish a backward-compatibility baseline.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S5.I1.ix3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">(c)</span> 
<div id="S5.I1.ix3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.I1.ix3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">CL-based base adapter <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite>. This adapter is trained using an InfoNCE-style contrastive objective <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>:</p>
</div>
<figure id="S5.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S5.T2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 2</span>: </span><span id="S5.T2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Compatibility results on MMEB benchmarks.<span id="S5.T2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> The numbers in parentheses indicate the number of sub-datasets in each category. We report Precision@1 as the evaluation metric. Other details are the same as in <a href="#S5.T1" title="In 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</span></span></figcaption>

<table id="S5.E9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S5.E9.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{CL}=-\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log\frac{\exp(\text{sim}(h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new}),\mathbf{x}_{i}^{old})/\tau)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}\exp(\text{sim}(h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new}),\mathbf{x}_{j}^{old})/\tau)}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo rspace="0em">=</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.055em">−</mo><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mi>N</mi></msup><mi>log</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>sim</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation <td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S5.I1.ix3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S5.I1.ix3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{sim}(\cdot,\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>sim</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{sim}(\cdot,\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes cosine similarity and <math id="S5.I1.ix3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> is the temperature parameter (set to 0.07). This loss maximizes similarity between the projected new embedding <math id="S5.I1.ix3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new})</annotation></semantics></math> and its corresponding old embedding <math id="S5.I1.ix3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{i}^{old}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{i}^{old}</annotation></semantics></math> (positive pair), while minimizing similarity with other old embeddings (negatives).
Note that our proposed regularization techniques can also be combined with this contrastive base adapter. We include these results in <a href="#Pt0.A2.T6" title="In B.6 Combination with CL-based adapter [] ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S6</span></a>.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>

</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S5.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We omit XBT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite> from the main tables for two reasons.
First, XBT requires LoRA-tuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>]</cite> of the new embedding model, making it an unfair comparison to our adapter-only setting.
Second, as detailed in <a href="#Pt0.A3" title="Appendix C Comparison with XBT [] ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>, XBT performs worse in our MLLM compatibility settings, even compared to other adapter-only baselines, likely because it disrupts the pre-trained representations of well-trained MLLMs.
Additional analyses and results are provided in S.M.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Main results</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S5.F2" title="In 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> provides an overview of backward compatibility performance across three representative model upgrade scenarios in image-text-based benchmarks; the y-axis shows the performance gap relative to the old model, with the black dashed line at zero indicating the old model’s performance.
Overall, MKP-Adapter (shown in red) consistently improves over the old model and all baseline adapters on both standard I2T/T2I retrieval and the more challenging MMEB benchmark, with average (across scenarios) gains of <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+5.43\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>5.43</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+5.43\%</annotation></semantics></math> on I2T, <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+7.63\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>7.63</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+7.63\%</annotation></semantics></math> on T2I, and <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+10.53\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>10.53</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+10.53\%</annotation></semantics></math> on MMEB.
In contrast, existing baselines often fail to preserve backward compatibility (<em id="S5.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">i.e</em>.<span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text"></span>, they underperform the old model itself).
Specifically, on standard I2T/T2I retrieval (<a href="#S5.F2" title="In 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and <a href="#S5.T1" title="In 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), CL-based adapters typically degrade I2T performance (<em id="S5.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g</em>.<span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text"></span>, in the CLIP<math id="S5.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>GME and CLIP<math id="S5.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>UniME scenarios), while <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L2</annotation></semantics></math>-based adapters (Base and EC-style) often degrade T2I performance.
On the other hand, MKP-Adapter consistently improves performance on both tasks, achieving substantial gains in the CLIP<math id="S5.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>UniME scenario (<math id="S5.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+7.96\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>7.96</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+7.96\%</annotation></semantics></math> on I2T and <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+10.6\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>10.6</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+10.6\%</annotation></semantics></math> on T2I on average).
On the MMEB benchmark (<a href="#S5.F2" title="In 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Fig.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> and <a href="#S5.T2" title="In item (c) ‣ 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), CL-based adapters generally outperform <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L2</annotation></semantics></math>-based ones, consistent with their stronger T2I performance in <a href="#S5.T1" title="In 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, as MMEB often involves text-heavy queries. However, they still fail to maintain backward compatibility in some scenarios (<em id="S5.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">e.g</em>.<span id="S5.SS2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text"></span>, CLIP<math id="S5.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>UniME).
In contrast, MKP-Adapter consistently achieves the strongest performance across upgrade scenarios, with particularly large gains in the CLIP<math id="S5.SS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math>UniME setting (averaging <math id="S5.SS2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+9.30\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>9.30</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+9.30\%</annotation></semantics></math> over the old model), showing robust backward compatibility and out-of-domain generalization.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We further report results on text-to-visual-document and text-to-video retrieval in <a href="#S5.T3" title="In 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.
MKP-Adapter achieves substantial gains on both tasks, demonstrating strong generalization (<math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+17.05\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>17.05</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+17.05\%</annotation></semantics></math> on visual documents and <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+4.80\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mn>4.80</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+4.80\%</annotation></semantics></math> on videos).
In this setting, <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L2</annotation></semantics></math>-based adapters perform significantly worse than on other benchmarks; we therefore adopt a contrastive learning (CL) objective as the base adapter.
<a href="#Pt0.A2.T6" title="In B.6 Combination with CL-based adapter [] ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S6</span></a> provides additional evidence that our method remains effective when combined with CL-based adapters, confirming the modularity and versatility of our approach. Further details are provided in S.M.</p>
</div>

<section id="S5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.3 </span>Ablation studies</h3>

<div id="S5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed components in <a href="#S5.T4" title="In 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, including the multi-level preservation losses (point-, distance-, and angle-wise) and the focal re-weighting strategy.
All adapters are trained on LLaVA-LCS under the same setup as in <a href="#S5.T1" title="In 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tabs.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and <a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ item (c) ‣ 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. We focus on the CLIP ViT-L/14 (old) <math id="S5.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> UniME (new) scenario, where the first row corresponds to the full model.
Removing any component consistently degrades performance across metrics, indicating complementary contributions.
In particular, removing the “distance loss” degrades standard I2T/T2I performance, whereas removing other components more strongly affects MMEB metrics.
Additional results in <a href="#Pt0.A2.T1" title="In B.2 More results on main ablations ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S1</span></a> and <a href="#Pt0.A2.T2" title="In B.2 More results on main ablations ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S2</span></a> analyze the standalone impact of each component.
Each preservation loss yields positive gains individually and complementary improvements when combined (<a href="#Pt0.A2.T1" title="In B.2 More results on main ablations ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S1</span></a>).
Focal re-weighting consistently improves performance across different loss combinations (<a href="#Pt0.A2.T2" title="In B.2 More results on main ablations ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S2</span></a>), demonstrating its robustness.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.4 </span>Analyses</h3>

<div id="S5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Impact of preservation loss]</span>
We validate our core hypothesis: whether our method preserves the representational quality of the new embeddings. To this end, we evaluate retrieval when both the query and database use the projected embeddings <math id="S5.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h(\mathbf{x}^{new})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h(\mathbf{x}^{new})</annotation></semantics></math> (rows 5-6), instead of using the original old embeddings in the database as in the standard BCT setting (rows 3-4).
If the similarity structure of the new embeddings is preserved after projection, the resulting performance should remain close to that of the new model and considerably exceed that of the old model.
As shown in the last row of <a href="#S5.T5" title="In 5.2 Main results ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, the projected embeddings from ours (row 6) achieve performance within 0.2 points of the new embedding model (row 2), indicating that MKP-Adapter preserves retrieval quality in the projected space and thus enables effective backward compatibility (row 4).</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Next, we analyze the trade-off between projection and preservation by varying <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>.
When <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, the base projection loss is removed, leading to near-zero performance, as expected.
Performance peaks around <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda\in[0.5,10]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mn>0.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda\in[0.5,10]</annotation></semantics></math>, while overly large values (<math id="S5.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda&gt;100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda&gt;100</annotation></semantics></math>) degrade results by over-emphasizing preservation. Our method remains stable across a broad moderate range, indicating robustness to <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>. Sensitivity to other hyperparameters, including the relative weights among preservation losses and the focal parameter <math id="S5.SS4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math>, is reported in <a href="#Pt0.A2.T10" title="In B.8 Hyper-parameters ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S10</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Adapter sizes and dataset scales]</span> Larger adapters yield slightly better results, but the overall trends remain consistent. Increasing the training data from 558k pairs (LLaVA-LCS) to 4M pairs (CC3M+SBU) provides only marginal gains, suggesting that our adapter design and a moderate-scale dataset are already sufficient to achieve strong and robust performance across benchmarks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">[Computational overhead] </span>
We first measure the inference cost of our adapter on a single A100 (40GB) with a batch size of 32. In the CLIP ViT-L/14 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite> to UniME (7B) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite> setting, our adapter adds only 0.25 ms of latency per batch (0.01% latency to the original backbone forward pass).
Training is also efficient, requiring less than 10 minutes per epoch on a 1M-sample dataset, whereas LoRA-tuning a 7B model typically takes over a day per epoch even on H100 GPUs.
Although we use 50 epochs by default, 10 epochs already achieve comparable performance (see S.M.), enabling complete training in 1–2 hours on 8 A100 GPUs. In contrast, backfilling even a moderate 5M-scale database takes about one day.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a practical adapter-only approach for achieving backward compatibility with MLLMs.
We devise multi-level preservation losses with focal re-weighting to retain the representational quality of new embeddings after projection.
Experiments across diverse modalities demonstrate strong backward compatibility with negligible latency and efficient training.</p>
</div>
</section>

<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:144%;">Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility<span id="p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">

<br class="ltx_break"></span></span></p>

<div id="p2" class="ltx_para ltx_align_center">
<p id="p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:144%;">Supplementary Material 
<br class="ltx_break"></span></p>
</div>
<section id="Pt0.A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Details on loss functions</h2>

<section id="Pt0.A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Details on preservation loss</h3>

<div id="Pt0.A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As described in <a href="#S4" title="4 Method ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, both the distance-wise and angle-wise preservation losses are composed of two parts: a global term and a local term. Each preservation loss is defined as the sum of these two components, as defined in <a href="#Pt0.A1.E10" title="In A.1 Details on preservation loss ‣ Appendix A Details on loss functions ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eqs.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S10</span></a> and <a href="#Pt0.A1.E13" title="Equation S13 ‣ A.1 Details on preservation loss ‣ Appendix A Details on loss functions ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S13</span></a>.
In the global distance-wise preservation loss (<a href="#Pt0.A1.E11" title="In A.1 Details on preservation loss ‣ Appendix A Details on loss functions ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S11</span></a>), index <math id="Pt0.A1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> denotes an anchor sample from the mini-batch, and <math id="Pt0.A1.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes another sample randomly drawn from the same mini-batch. In contrast, the local distance-wise preservation loss (<a href="#Pt0.A1.E12" title="In A.1 Details on preservation loss ‣ Appendix A Details on loss functions ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S12</span></a>) considers the <math id="Pt0.A1.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> nearest neighbors of each anchor and enforces the preservation of their relative distance relationships. We select nearest neighbors in the new embedding space, since it preserves better semantic structure, which aligns with our core motivation. We set <math id="Pt0.A1.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m=100</annotation></semantics></math> in all experiments.</p>
</div>
<div id="Pt0.A1.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="Pt0.A1.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

</table>
</div>

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(S12)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="Pt0.A1.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A1.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Similar to the distance-wise loss, the global angle-wise preservation loss in <a href="#Pt0.A1.E14" title="In A.1 Details on preservation loss ‣ Appendix A Details on loss functions ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S14</span></a> follows the same indexing scheme: <math id="Pt0.A1.SS1.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="j" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>j</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">j</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the anchor sample, while <math id="Pt0.A1.SS1.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="Pt0.A1.SS1.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> denote randomly sampled samples from the mini-batch that are used to form angular relationships. The local angle-wise loss, defined in <a href="#Pt0.A1.E15" title="In A.1 Details on preservation loss ‣ Appendix A Details on loss functions ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S15</span></a>, considers the <math id="Pt0.A1.SS1.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> nearest neighbors of each anchor. To control computational cost, we limit the number of sampled pairs <math id="Pt0.A1.SS1.p5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(i,k)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(i,k)</annotation></semantics></math> per anchor to 32 for both the global and local angle-wise losses.</p>
</div>
<div id="Pt0.A1.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para">

</section>
<section id="Pt0.A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Details on focal re-weighting strategy</h3>

<div id="Pt0.A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Similar to the point-wise preservation loss in <a href="#S4.E7" title="In 4.3 Focal re-weighting strategy ‣ 4 Method ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>, we compute the focal weights for the distance-wise and angle-wise preservation losses based on their respective preservation errors, as defined below:</p>
</div>
<div id="Pt0.A1.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="Pt0.A1.E16" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

&amp;w_{ij}=\left(\frac{\Delta_{ij}}{\bar{\Delta}_{distance}}\right)^{\gamma},\quad\bar{\Delta}_{distance}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}}\Delta_{ij}.\end{split}" display="block" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi></mrow></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{split}\mathcal{L}_{distance}^{focal}&amp;=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}}w_{ij}\Delta_{ij},\\
\text{where}\quad&amp;\Delta_{ij}=\left|\text{Dist}(h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new}),h(\mathbf{x}_{j}^{new}))-\text{Dist}(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{new},\mathbf{x}_{j}^{new})\right|,\\
&amp;w_{ij}=\left(\frac{\Delta_{ij}}{\bar{\Delta}_{distance}}\right)^{\gamma},\quad\bar{\Delta}_{distance}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}}\Delta_{ij}.\end{split}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(S16)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>

</section>
</section>
<section id="Pt0.A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Additional details and results</h2>

<section id="Pt0.A2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.1 </span>Additional implementation details</h3>

<div id="Pt0.A2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use Pytorch 2.4 with CUDA 12.5.
We use CLIP ViT-L/14 with 768-dimensional embeddings. E5-V and UniME share the LLaVA-1.6 (7B) backbone <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>]</cite> and produce 4096-dimensional embeddings, whereas GME (7B) is based on Qwen2-VL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite> and produces 3584-dimensional embeddings.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Pt0.A2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.2 </span>More results on main ablations</h3>

<div id="Pt0.A2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further analyze the standalone impact of each preservation loss and the focal re-weighting strategy in <a href="#Pt0.A2.T1" title="In B.2 More results on main ablations ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S1</span></a> and <a href="#Pt0.A2.T2" title="In B.2 More results on main ablations ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S2</span></a>. As shown in <a href="#Pt0.A2.T1" title="In B.2 More results on main ablations ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S1</span></a>, each component provides distinct and complementary benefits. The point-wise preservation loss mainly improves MMEB, while the distance-wise preservation loss primarily boosts I2T and T2I performance, and the angle-wise preservation loss yields more balanced improvements across metrics. Combining all three preservation losses consistently achieves the best overall performance, highlighting their complementary nature.
In <a href="#Pt0.A2.T2" title="In B.2 More results on main ablations ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S2</span></a>, we observe that across various combinations of preservation loss variants, incorporating the focal re-weighting strategy enhances performance on average (with an overall improvement of +2.11%), demonstrating its effectiveness.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Pt0.A2.T1" class="ltx_table">

<section id="Pt0.A2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.3 </span>Batch size ablation</h3>

<div id="Pt0.A2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate our method across various batch sizes and find that performance remains stable. While the CL-based method benefits slightly from larger batch sizes by leveraging more negative samples in contrastive learning, the overall impact on performance is marginal.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Pt0.A2.T3" class="ltx_table">

</section>
<section id="Pt0.A2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.4 </span>Adapter size ablation</h3>

<div id="Pt0.A2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in <a href="#Pt0.A2.T4" title="In B.4 Adapter size ablation ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S4</span></a>, increasing the hidden size yields marginal gains, suggesting that the current adapter capacity is sufficient for learning the mapping.</p>
</div>

Details are the same as in <a href="#S5.T1" title="In 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. </span></span></figcaption>

</section>
<section id="Pt0.A2.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.5 </span>Different base adapters</h3>

<div id="Pt0.A2.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A2.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Since we employ a single adapter shared across all modalities, we compare this design against modality-specific adapters with various loss configurations in <a href="#Pt0.A2.T5" title="In B.5 Different base adapters ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S5</span></a>. As shown, the unified single adapter achieves slightly better performance than separate adapters, leading us to adopt this design as our default. Additionally, <math id="Pt0.A2.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L2</annotation></semantics></math> loss generally outperforms <math id="Pt0.A2.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L1</annotation></semantics></math> loss. While the CL-based adapter performs competitively in the E5-V to UniME-7B setting, as observed in the main results, it excels primarily in T2I retrieval but falls short in I2T retrieval in other model variations. In contrast, our method consistently achieves superior performance across all scenarios.</p>
</div>

</section>
<section id="Pt0.A2.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.6 </span>Combination with CL-based adapter <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite></h3>

<div id="Pt0.A2.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A2.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We additionally evaluate a variant in which a contrastive learning (CL) loss is used for the base adapter. Specifically, in place of the base adapter loss in <a href="#S3.E1" title="In 3.2 Base adapter ‣ 3 Problem Settings ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we use the CL objective defined in <a href="#S5.E9" title="In item (c) ‣ 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>. For the point-wise preservation loss, instead of the <math id="Pt0.A2.SS6.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L2</annotation></semantics></math> formulation in <a href="#S4.E2" title="In 4.2 Multi-level preservation loss ‣ 4 Method ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we adopt a CL-based variant that treats <math id="Pt0.A2.SS6.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(g(h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{new}})),\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{new}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mtext>new</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mtext>new</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(g(h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{new}})),\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{new}})</annotation></semantics></math> as a positive pair. Note that the remaining preservation losses are applied in their original form.
As shown in <a href="#Pt0.A2.T6" title="In B.6 Combination with CL-based adapter [] ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S6</span></a>, our method remains effective under this configuration, demonstrating the generalizability of our proposed loss design beyond the <math id="Pt0.A2.SS6.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L2</annotation></semantics></math>-based adapter.</p>
</div>

<td id="Pt0.A2.T6.6.1.11.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;">92.00</td>
<td id="Pt0.A2.T6.6.1.11.10" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;"><span id="Pt0.A2.T6.6.1.11.10.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">83.43</span></td>

</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="Pt0.A2.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.7 </span>Use of composition data</h3>

<div id="Pt0.A2.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A2.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As described in <a href="#S5" title="5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we additionally use composition data consisting of fused image–text inputs. Since dual-encoder models such as CLIP cannot directly process image–text compositions, we approximate them during training by summing the corresponding image and text features to construct a composite embedding.
As shown in <a href="#Pt0.A2.T7" title="In B.7 Use of composition data ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S7</span></a>, incorporating composition data improves the performance of <math id="Pt0.A2.SS7.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L2</annotation></semantics></math>- and EC-style adapters in the E5-V <math id="Pt0.A2.SS7.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> UniME compatibility setting on the MMEB benchmark. We therefore adopt composition data as part of our default experimental setup to avoid underestimating baseline performance.
At the same time, as reported in <a href="#Pt0.A2.T8" title="In B.7 Use of composition data ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S8</span></a>, our method consistently achieves considerable improvements both with and without composition data, indicating that its effectiveness does not rely on this design choice.</p>
</div>
<div id="Pt0.A2.SS7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A2.SS7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">When using a dual-tower model (CLIP) as the old model in image–text benchmarks, we employ separate reverse adapters <math id="Pt0.A2.SS7.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> for each modality (image and text). The composition input is fed into the adapter for text modality.
Empirically, we observe that using separate modality-specific adapters <math id="Pt0.A2.SS7.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> versus a single shared reverse adapter <math id="Pt0.A2.SS7.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> results in only marginal performance differences.
We use the modality-specific setup as our default, while noting that a single shared reverse adapter <math id="Pt0.A2.SS7.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g</annotation></semantics></math> achieves comparable performance in most cases.
For the main adapter <math id="Pt0.A2.SS7.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>h</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h</annotation></semantics></math>, we always use a single unified adapter.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Pt0.A2.T7" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="Pt0.A2.T7.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table S7</span>: </span><span id="Pt0.A2.T7.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Inclusion of composition data.<span id="Pt0.A2.T7.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Details are the same as in <a href="#S5.T2" title="In item (c) ‣ 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. </span></span></figcaption>
