</section>
<section id="Pt0.A2.SS8" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.8 </span>Hyper-parameters</h3>

<div id="Pt0.A2.SS8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A2.SS8.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#Pt0.A2.T9" title="In B.8 Hyper-parameters ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S9</span></a> presents the full results corresponding to the figures in the main paper. As discussed therein, our method exhibits robust performance across varying values of <math id="Pt0.A2.SS8.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>, demonstrating its practical advantage for hyperparameter selection. We further evaluate performance with varying focal parameter <math id="Pt0.A2.SS8.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> and different weightings among the preservation loss terms in <a href="#Pt0.A2.T10" title="In B.8 Hyper-parameters ‣ Appendix B Additional details and results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S10</span></a>. In the preservation loss weight ablation, <math id="Pt0.A2.SS8.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(a,b,c)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(a,b,c)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the weights assigned to the point-, distance-, and angle-wise preservation losses, respectively.
While some variation is observed, performance remains consistently strong across all configurations and continues to outperform the baselines by a clear margin.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Pt0.A2.T9" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="Pt0.A2.T9.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table S9</span>: </span><span id="Pt0.A2.T9.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Analyses on <math id="Pt0.A2.T9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math><span id="Pt0.A2.T9.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. Details are the same as in <a href="#S5.T1" title="In 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. </span></span></figcaption>
<div id="Pt0.A2.T9.6" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:107.5pt;vertical-align:-52.1pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-82.5pt,25.7pt) scale(0.67658793670861,0.67658793670861) ;">
<table id="Pt0.A2.T9.6.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">

</section>
<section id="Pt0.A2.SS9" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">B.9 </span>Exclusion of UniME in <a href="#S5.T3" title="In 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</h3>

<div id="Pt0.A2.SS9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A2.SS9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">UniME is excluded because, as a new model, it does not achieve better performance than potential old models (CLIP or E5-V) on the visual document and video benchmark; not a proper model update scenario.
We believe this is likely because UniME is built on a LLaVA-NeXT backbone, which is not explicitly pre-trained on video data, whereas GME leverages Qwen2-VL, which is pre-trained on both visual document and video data and further fine-tuned on larger-scale and more diverse datasets to serve as an embedding model.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="Pt0.A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Comparison with XBT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite></h2>

<div id="Pt0.A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Before presenting our results, we describe XBT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>]</cite> in more detail. XBT is a two-stage approach: (1) it first pre-trains an adapter using text-only data for training efficiency, and (2) it then LoRA-tunes the backbone of the new model using a contrastive learning objective.
In the first stage, XBT trains the adapter with the contrastive loss in <a href="#S5.E9" title="In item (c) ‣ 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Eq.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>, where <math id="Pt0.A3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{new}}),\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{old}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mtext>new</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>i</mi><mtext>old</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(h(\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{new}}),\mathbf{x}_{i}^{\text{old}})</annotation></semantics></math> is treated as a positive pair. XBT uses only text data for efficiency. After the adapter is trained, XBT proceeds to the second stage, where it LoRA-tunes the backbone of the new model while keeping the adapter frozen (except for the LayerNorm parameters). This LoRA-tuning uses a cross-modal contrastive learning objective that treats <math id="Pt0.A3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(h(\mathbf{x}_{i,\mathrm{img}}^{\text{new}}),h(\mathbf{x}_{i,\mathrm{txt}}^{\text{new}}))" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>img</mi></mrow><mtext>new</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>txt</mi></mrow><mtext>new</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(h(\mathbf{x}_{i,\mathrm{img}}^{\text{new}}),h(\mathbf{x}_{i,\mathrm{txt}}^{\text{new}}))</annotation></semantics></math> as a positive pair.</p>
</div>
<div id="Pt0.A3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate XBT in our MLLM setting using the LLaVA-LCS dataset for training and observe degraded performance compared to even base adapters. We additionally experiment with a larger dataset (CC3M+SBU, approximately 4M image–text pairs) to match the original training scale of XBT, using the cleaned captions for CC3M to more closely follow XBT’s default training setup. As shown in <a href="#Pt0.A3.T11" title="In Appendix C Comparison with XBT [] ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S11</span></a>, the performance is still even weaker than old embedding models. All reported results correspond to the best-performing configurations over sweeps of LoRA hyperparameters (including different ranks and <math id="Pt0.A3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> values) and learning rates.</p>
</div>
<figure id="Pt0.A3.T11" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="Pt0.A3.T11.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table S11</span>: </span><span id="Pt0.A3.T11.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Comparison with XBT.<span id="Pt0.A3.T11.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Details are the same as in <a href="#S5.T1" title="In 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. </span></span></figcaption>

<td id="Pt0.A3.T11.6.1.10.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_b" style="padding-left:3.0pt;padding-right:3.0pt;">65.65</td></tr>

</table>
</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="Pt0.A3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We attribute this inferior performance of XBT in our MLLM setting to a fundamental difference in the difficulty of applying LoRA-tuning to CLIP- and MLLM-based embedding models. We hypothesize that the success of XBT in its original XBT paper setup (<em id="Pt0.A3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">i.e</em>.<span id="Pt0.A3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text"></span>, the CLIP-to-CLIP upgrade scenario) mainly arises from improving the new embedding model itself via LoRA-tuning. Specifically, as reported in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, Table 1]</cite>, the retrieval performance of the LoRA-tuned new model (even when evaluated in the projected space) substantially exceeds that of the original new model, with gains of <math id="Pt0.A3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+15.71" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>15.71</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+15.71</annotation></semantics></math> in T2I R@1 and <math id="Pt0.A3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="+3.93" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>3.93</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">+3.93</annotation></semantics></math> in I2T R@1 on the NoCaps dataset.
Such improvements from LoRA-tuning with clean captions are plausible for CLIP, which was originally pre-trained on noisy, web-scale data. Prior work has shown that training with higher-quality captions can significantly improve performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="Pt0.A3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">However, this strategy appears ineffective for MLLMs. MLLM-based embedding models are typically already obtained by LoRA tuning large base MLLMs on large-scale, carefully curated datasets using tailored training strategies such as hard-negative mining. Consequently, additional LoRA-tuning with a simple contrastive objective on moderate-scale datasets provides little benefit and can even be detrimental.
To examine this, in <a href="#Pt0.A3.T11" title="In Appendix C Comparison with XBT [] ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S11</span></a> (rows 5 and 6), we directly apply LoRA fine-tuning to the new model backbone in its original embedding space, without using the adapter, which constitutes an easier setting for LoRA than LoRA-tuning in the projected space. As shown in <a href="#Pt0.A3.T11" title="In Appendix C Comparison with XBT [] ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S11</span></a> (rows 5 and 6), the resulting LoRA-tuned embeddings fail to improve performance and in some cases degrade it, highlighting the risk of further updating the backbone of MLLM-based embedding models.</p>
</div>
<div id="Pt0.A3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Since LoRA fine-tuning degrades the performance of the new embedding model even in its own space, this degradation is likely to be amplified in the projected space used for backward compatibility. As a result, the projected embeddings become noisier inputs to the adapter, further compromising compatibility, consistent with our empirical findings. These results underscore the difficulty of applying additional LoRA tuning in MLLM settings: modifying the new model backbone risks degrading its original performance unless substantially more sophisticated data curation and training strategies are employed.
In contrast, our adapter-only approach achieves effective backward compatibility without requiring large-scale, carefully curated additional training data or risking degradation of the base model’s performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Pt0.A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Computational analyses</h2>

<div id="Pt0.A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to adapter training, our pipeline requires a one-time preprocessing stage consisting of feature extraction and neighbor mining, which takes approximately 4–5 hours on 8 A100 GPUs.
We argue that this is a highly efficient one-time investment when compared to the alternative of fine-tuning the backbone (<span id="Pt0.A4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">e.g.</span>, via LoRA).
Once extracted, the MKP-Adapter can be trained very efficiently (approximately 1–2 hours). BCT approaches using LoRA instead require a forward and backward pass through the massive MLLM backbone for every training step. On the same 1M sample dataset, a single epoch of LoRA tuning exceeds 24 hours on 8 H100 GPUs.</p>
</div>
<div id="Pt0.A4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As discussed in <a href="#S5.SS4" title="5.4 Analyses ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Sec.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.4</span></a>, although our default setup uses 50 training epochs, our method achieves sufficient performance when trained for only 10 epochs, with a total training time of approximately 1–2 hours on a 1M-sample dataset in the CLIP ViT/L-14 <math id="Pt0.A4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> UniME (7B) setting. As shown in <a href="#Pt0.A4.T12" title="In Appendix D Computational analyses ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S12</span></a>, while training for 50 epochs yields slightly better performance, the 10-epoch results are on par with those obtained with full 50-epoch training in most cases.</p>
</div>

<section id="Pt0.A4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.1 </span>Additional scaling experiments</h3>

<div id="Pt0.A4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct experiments by sub-sampling at varying scales (5k–500k) from LLaVA-LCS.
As shown in <a href="#Pt0.A4.T13" title="In D.1 Additional scaling experiments ‣ Appendix D Computational analyses ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S13</span></a>, the trend is consistent with <a href="#S5.T6" title="In 5.2 Main results ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>: a moderate dataset scale is sufficient, with performance saturating at around 200k samples.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="Pt0.A4.T13.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table S13</span>: </span><span id="Pt0.A4.T13.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Additional data scale experiments with LLaVA-LCS. </span></figcaption>

<table id="Pt0.A4.T13.5.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">

<td id="Pt0.A4.T13.5.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="Pt0.A4.T13.5.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:120%;">5k</span></td>
<td id="Pt0.A4.T13.5.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t"><span id="Pt0.A4.T13.5.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:120%;">10k</span></td>

<section id="Pt0.A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Additional evaluation</h2>

<section id="Pt0.A5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.1 </span>Five random seed results</h3>

<div id="Pt0.A5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We additionally calculate results of “MKP-Adapter” and “Base-adapter” from five different random seeds under the same evaluation setup as <a href="#S5.T1" title="In 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. The standard deviation of the average I2T/T2I R@1 is below <math id="Pt0.A5.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.2\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0.2</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.2\%</annotation></semantics></math> points, showing that the observed improvement is consistent.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Pt0.A5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.2 </span>Additional R@10 results corresponding to <a href="#S5.T1" title="In 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a></h3>

<div id="Pt0.A5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To provide a more comprehensive evaluation beyond R@1, in <a href="#Pt0.A5.T14" title="In E.2 Additional R@10 results corresponding to ‣ Appendix E Additional evaluation ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">S14</span></a>, we report R@10 results under the same setting as <a href="#S5.T1" title="In 5.1 Experimental settings ‣ 5 Experimental Results ‣ Multi-modal Knowledge Preserving Adapter for Embedding Backward Compatibility" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Tab.</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, where trends are consistent with R@1.</p>

</section>
<section id="Pt0.A5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.3 </span>Large retrieval evaluation (COCO val entire set)</h3>

<div id="Pt0.A5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Pt0.A5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We also evaluate our method on a large-scale retrieval setting. In contrast to the standard MS-COCO Karpathy test split (5,000 images and 25,000 captions), we use the entire COCO 2014 validation set, comprising 40,373 images and 201,865 captions. Note that while the original validation set contains 40,504 images, we exclude images that do not have exactly five corresponding captions for a fair comparison. Our method again demonstrates strong performance in this large-scale setting, which more closely resembles real-world retrieval applications.</p>
</div>
